questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the head of a pin?

options.why: Chose the unit that suits a stamp or a phone screen, which are far wider than a pin head.
Chose a room-sized unit, which would make the pin head a decimal with several leading zeros.

questions.solution_text:
A pin head is about a millimetre across.
The square millimetre is the square that matches a surface that small.
$\text{mm}^2$

questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the state of Queensland?

options.why: Chose the unit used for paddocks, which would give a state an area running into the millions.
Chose a room-sized unit, which would give a state an area with more than twelve digits.

questions.solution_text:
Queensland is a very large region.
Square kilometres give a convenient number and are commonly used for states.
$\text{km}^2$

questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the top surface of a single bed?

options.why: Chose a unit suited to tiny surfaces, giving an unnecessarily large count for a bed.
Chose a unit suited to large areas of land, making a bed's area a very small decimal.
Chose a unit suited to large regions, far larger than the surface of a bed.

questions.solution_text:
A single bed is roughly a metre wide and a couple of metres long.
Square metres give a convenient number for its top surface.
$\text{m}^2$

questions.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for a large wheat paddock?

options.why: Chose a unit suited to small objects, giving an enormous count for farmland.
Chose a unit suited to tiny surfaces, giving an enormous count for a paddock.
Chose a unit suited to rooms and courts, giving a much larger count than hectares for a large paddock.

questions.solution_text:
A large wheat paddock is a large area of farmland.
Hectares are commonly used for farmland and give a convenient number.
ha

questions.question_text:
A farm's area is recorded as $250\,000\text{ m}^2$.
Which unit would present this area best?

options.why: Kept the recorded unit even though a six-digit count is hard to compare with other farms.
Jumped to the region-sized unit, giving a decimal well below $1$ for a single farm.

questions.solution_text:
A six-digit count of square metres is accurate but hard to picture.
Hectares are the unit used for farmland and turn the same area into a short whole number.
ha

questions.question_text:
Tom writes the area of his phone screen as $0.0104\text{ m}^2$.
Which unit would present this area best?

options.why: Dropped two units down the ladder, turning a hand-sized screen into a five-digit count.
Kept a unit much larger than a phone screen, leaving the area as a small decimal rather than a convenient number of square centimetres.

questions.solution_text:
A square metre is far bigger than a phone screen, so the reading sits well below $1$.
A screen is about $10$ cm by $10$ cm, so the square centimetre gives a readable whole number.
$\text{cm}^2$

questions.question_text:
A council report records four areas: a postage stamp on a letter, a lounge-room rug, the local sports ground and the whole council area.
Which set of units is most appropriate, in that order?

options.why: These choices give unnecessarily large numbers for the larger areas, especially the sports ground and whole council area.
Square metres give a large number for the sports ground, and hectares give a much larger number than square kilometres for the whole council area.
Jumped to square kilometres for the sports ground, giving an area far below $1$.

questions.solution_text:
A stamp is a few centimetres each way: $\text{cm}^2$.
A rug is a couple of metres each way: $\text{m}^2$.
A sports ground is a large area of land: ha.
A whole council area is a large region: $\text{km}^2$.
These units suit the size and context and give convenient numbers.
